plain_title: A dementia that changes personality or language first
one_liner: A dementia starting in the front and side parts of the brain, affecting behaviour, personality, or language before memory.
in_simple_words: Frontotemporal dementia damages the frontal and temporal lobes, which handle behaviour, judgment, empathy, and language. Unlike Alzheimer's, it usually starts between 45 and 65 and memory is often spared early on. In the behavioural form, a person becomes socially inappropriate, impulsive, apathetic, or loses empathy, which families often mistake for depression. In the language forms, speech or understanding of words gradually breaks down. It's often misdiagnosed for years; support and planning help greatly.
what_it_can_feel_like: My husband started making crude jokes at work and spending our savings. We thought it was a breakdown. It was FTD.
She lost the word for 'fork', then 'daughter'. Her memory of us was fine. That's what made it so cruel.
The AFTD group was the first place anyone had heard of it.
common_signs: Changes in personality, social behaviour, or judgment: tactlessness, impulsivity, apathy, loss of empathy
Or: progressive difficulty with speech, naming, or understanding words
Compulsive or repetitive behaviours, changes in eating
Memory relatively preserved in the early stages
Usual onset between 45 and 65, often misdiagnosed as psychiatric illness
Lack of insight into the changes

myths_vs_facts.myth: Dementia always starts with memory loss.
myths_vs_facts.fact: FTD often starts with behaviour or language changes while memory stays intact, which is why it's missed.

myths_vs_facts.myth: The person is being deliberately rude or selfish.
myths_vs_facts.fact: The disease damages the brain regions that control social behaviour and empathy. The person usually can't see the change.

myths_vs_facts.myth: It's a rare condition that only affects the very old.
myths_vs_facts.fact: FTD is one of the commonest dementias in people under 65.

how_common.plain: Frontotemporal dementia is uncommon overall but is among the most common dementias in people under 65, where it may account for 1 in 10 to 1 in 5 cases.
how_common.figure: Estimated 2–10 per 100,000 in the general population; roughly 10–20% of dementia under 65 (reviews)

what_helps.plain_summary: There's no medication that slows FTD yet, and Alzheimer's drugs don't help. Care focuses on managing behaviour with structure, routine, and environment; speech and language therapy for language forms; occupational therapy; and sometimes medication for specific symptoms like agitation or compulsions, prescribed and monitored by a doctor. Because onset is often in working life, support with employment, finances, and family, and early legal planning, is vital. Carer support is essential; FTD is especially hard on families.
evidence_based_options: Specialist diagnosis, including genetic counselling where relevant
Behavioural and environmental strategies; structure and routine
Speech and language therapy for language variants
Medication for specific symptoms where needed, prescribed and monitored by a doctor; carer support
self_help_that_supports_care: Protecting finances early, with legal advice
Not taking personality changes personally, however hard
FTD-specific carer groups, which understand behaviour others don't

when_to_reach_out: If a person in midlife shows striking changes in personality, behaviour, or language that aren't like them, especially with little insight, ask for a neurology or memory clinic referral and mention frontotemporal dementia.
is_not: Depression, bipolar disorder, late-onset psychosis, and Alzheimer's can look similar; careful assessment tells them apart. A midlife change in behaviour with full insight is unlikely to be FTD.
hope_note: Families facing FTD find strength in each other. Specialist support turns an isolating, misunderstood illness into one that can be faced together.

content_notes: Site-wide crisis link stays one tap away.

sub_sections.title: Variants
sub_sections.text: Behavioural variant (changes in conduct and personality) and language variants (primary progressive aphasia: semantic, non-fluent, and logopenic types). Some people also develop motor neurone disease or movement disorders.
